1.1:
Defining AI

There is no single agreed definition of artificial intelligence, but most definitions share one idea. In everyday terms, artificial intelligence (AI) is the ability of computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognising speech, understanding language, identifying objects in images, making predictions or producing text.

A more technical definition describes AI as systems that take in information from their environment, find patterns in it, and use those patterns to make predictions, recommendations, decisions or new content in pursuit of a goal. The emphasis here is on learning patterns from data and acting on them, rather than on “thinking” in a human sense.

Intelligence versus automation

Not every computer program is AI. A calculator follows fixed instructions: the same input always produces the same output, and the program never improves. This is automation. An AI system, by contrast, handles situations its designers did not list one by one. A spam filter, for example, was never given a complete list of every spam message; it learned the features that spam messages tend to share and applies that learning to messages it has never seen.

ExampleA calculator; a school fees payment formA spam filter; a voice assistant; a chat assistant

The last row of the table matters most for users. Because AI works with probabilities, its outputs are usually useful and occasionally wrong, sometimes confidently so. This theme returns throughout the course.

AI in daily life

Much of the AI people use is invisible. Face unlock on a phone uses image recognition. Banking apps flag unusual transactions as possible fraud. Map apps predict journey times from the movement of other users. Social media and video platforms recommend content based on what you and similar users have watched. Keyboards predict your next word, and translation apps convert speech and text between languages. More recently, chat assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot have made AI something people talk to directly.

AI, machine learning and deep learning

Nigeria’s technology sector already uses AI in several areas. Fintech companies use it to detect fraud and assess creditworthiness, often for customers without formal credit histories. 1.3:
Public discussion of AI swings between excitement and fear, and several myths have become widespread. Each contains a grain of truth, which is why they are persuasive, but each is misleading.

MythReality
AI thinks and understands like humans.AI systems process patterns in data. A chat assistant produces fluent language by predicting likely words, not by understanding meaning as a person does. Fluency is not the same as comprehension.
AI is always right.AI makes errors, including confident, detailed and entirely fabricated answers. Every important AI output needs checking.
AI will replace all jobs.AI automates particular tasks, not whole jobs. Most jobs will change, some will shrink, and new ones will appear. People who can work well with AI will be in demand.
AI is neutral and objective.AI learns from data produced by people and chosen by people. It can repeat and even amplify existing biases.
AI is only for experts.Most AI tools are now used through ordinary language, on phones, with no programming. The skills that matter most are clear communication and critical judgement.

Why fluent language is persuasive

The first two myths are especially important for students. When an AI tool answers in clear, grammatical, well-organised language, people naturally assume it knows what it is talking about, because in humans fluency usually signals knowledge. With AI, that signal is unreliable. A chat assistant can produce a polished paragraph that cites a textbook that does not exist, or a formula with one sign reversed. Throughout this course, treat fluency as a reason to read carefully, not a reason to trust.

Key idea

AI predicts; it does not know. Treat its output as a capable first draft that you are responsible for checking.
1.4:
AI literacy is the knowledge and judgement needed to understand, use and evaluate AI responsibly. It does not mean being able to build AI systems. It means knowing what AI can and cannot do, using it effectively, recognising its risks, and making informed decisions about when to rely on it.

For students

AI can explain difficult ideas, generate practice questions and help organise research. It can also produce wrong information, fabricated references and work that breaches academic integrity rules. AI-literate students gain the benefits while avoiding the traps, and they learn more, not less, from using AI.

For future teachers

Your future learners will grow up with AI. They will use it for homework whether or not they are taught how. Teachers who understand AI can use it to plan and differentiate lessons, design assessments that still measure real learning, and guide learners to use AI honestly and critically. Teachers who do not understand it will struggle to do any of these.

For citizens

AI increasingly shapes the information people see, the services they receive and the decisions made about them, from loan applications to news feeds. AI-generated images, audio and video can be used to spread misinformation or to commit fraud. AI literacy helps citizens question what they see, protect their personal data, and take part in public debate about how AI should be governed.

Key idea

AI literacy is not about building AI. It is about understanding, using and questioning it well.
2.1:
Precursors

The idea of machines that imitate human abilities is ancient. Many cultures told stories of artificial beings, and craftsmen built automata, mechanical figures that moved by clockwork. The more direct foundations of AI came from two developments. The first was formal logic, which showed that reasoning could be written as precise rules. The second was computing. In the nineteenth century, Charles Babbage designed a general-purpose mechanical computer, the Analytical Engine, and Ada Lovelace wrote what is often described as the first computer program for it. Lovelace also argued that such a machine could only do what it was instructed to do, an early statement of a debate that continues today.

Alan Turing

The British mathematician Alan Turing laid much of the theoretical groundwork for computing in the 1930s and 1940s. In his 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, he asked whether machines could think. Because “thinking” is hard to define, he proposed a practical test instead, now known as the Turing Test: if a person holding a text conversation cannot reliably tell whether they are talking to a machine or a human, the machine could be said to show intelligent behaviour.

The Turing Test has been influential but is widely criticised. Modern chat assistants can often pass informal versions of it, yet this shows that they produce convincing language, not that they understand. The test measures imitation, not intelligence.

The Dartmouth Workshop (1956)

The field of AI is usually dated to a summer research workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States in 1956. Its organisers, including John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky, proposed that “every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it”. McCarthy coined the term artificial intelligence for the proposal. The workshop brought together the researchers who would lead the field for decades.
2.2:
Early optimism

The first two decades of AI research focused on symbolic AI: representing knowledge as symbols and rules, and manipulating them with logic. Early programs proved mathematical theorems, played draughts and chess, and held simple conversations. ELIZA (1966), a program that imitated a counsellor by rephrasing users’ statements as questions, surprised many people who used it, even though it understood nothing. Researchers made bold predictions that human-level AI was only a few decades away.

The first AI winter

By the 1970s, it was clear that the early successes did not scale. Programs that worked in small, controlled “toy” problems failed in the messy real world. Computers lacked the memory and speed that more ambitious systems needed, and translating language turned out to be far harder than expected. Governments in the United States and the United Kingdom cut funding, and the period that followed became known as the first AI winter.

Expert systems

AI revived in the 1980s with expert systems: programs that captured the knowledge of human experts as large sets of if-then rules. A medical expert system, for example, might contain hundreds of rules of the form “if the patient has symptom A and test result B, then consider condition C”. Expert systems were used commercially for tasks such as configuring computer orders and assessing loans.

The second winter

Expert systems proved brittle. They could not handle cases their rules did not cover, and they were expensive to build and maintain, because every rule had to be written and updated by hand. When the market for specialised AI hardware collapsed in the late 1980s, a second AI winter followed. These cycles hold a lesson for today: impressive demonstrations do not always become reliable tools, and predictions about AI have often been too optimistic about timing.
2.3:
From rules to data

From the 1990s, AI research shifted from writing rules to learning from data. Instead of telling a computer how to recognise a spam email, researchers gave it thousands of examples labelled “spam” and “not spam” and let statistical methods find the patterns. This approach, machine learning, handled messy real-world data far better than hand-written rules, and it improved as more data became available.

The transformer

In 2017, researchers at Google published a paper titled “Attention Is All You Need”, which introduced the transformer, a neural-network design that processes all the words in a passage together and learns which words relate to which. Transformers could be trained efficiently on enormous amounts of text, and they became the foundation of large language models (LLMs), the technology behind today’s chat assistants.

ChatGPT and the generative AI wave

OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public in November 2022. It was not the first large language model, but it was the first that millions of people could use freely through a simple chat window, and it reached an estimated 100 million users within about two months. Other companies quickly released competing assistants and image generators, and generative AI features began appearing in search engines, office software, phones and social media apps.

3.1:
Narrow AI

Narrow AI (also called weak AI) performs a specific task or a limited range of tasks. A face-recognition system recognises faces; it cannot translate a sentence or plan a route. Every AI system in use today is narrow AI. Even chat assistants, which can discuss many topics and perform many tasks, are narrow in an important sense: they generate text and related outputs, they have no independent goals, and they fail in ways that reveal they lack general understanding.

General AI

Artificial general intelligence (AGI) refers to a hypothetical system that could learn and perform any intellectual task a human can, and transfer what it learns from one area to another as flexibly as people do. Some technology companies state that building AGI is their goal, and some researchers believe it could arrive within years; others think it is decades away or doubt it will be achieved with current methods. There is not even full agreement on how AGI should be defined or recognised.

Superintelligence

Superintelligence refers to a hypothetical AI that would far exceed human abilities in almost every area. It is speculative, but it is discussed seriously because of the questions it raises: how humans would keep control over systems more capable than themselves, and whose values such systems would serve. These questions are part of the field known as AI safety.

3.2:
Rule-based systems

A rule-based system follows if-then rules written by people. It is transparent, because you can read exactly why it made a decision, and it behaves predictably. But it is brittle: it cannot cope with situations its rules do not cover, and writing enough rules for a complex task is slow and often impossible.

Machine learning systems

A machine learning system learns patterns from examples. Instead of writing rules, developers provide data, and the system works out the patterns itself. It copes much better with variety and messy real-world input, and it can improve with more data. The trade-courseIds are that it needs a lot of good data, its reasoning is harder to inspect, and it can learn the wrong patterns.

Consider marking a short-answer question, “Name the process by which plants make food”:

Hybrid systems

Many real products are hybrid. A banking app might use machine learning to flag unusual transactions but apply fixed rules, such as a daily transfer limit, that must always hold. A chat assistant uses a learned language model but may also have rules about what content it will not produce. Combining the two can give the flexibility of learning with the reliability of rules.
3.3:
Data, features and labels

Machine learning starts with data: a collection of examples. Each example is described by features, the pieces of information the system can use. In supervised learning (see 3.4), each example also has a label, the correct answer the system should learn to predict.

During training, the system looks at many labelled examples and adjusts itself to capture the relationship between features and labels, for example that low attendance combined with few submitted assignments is strongly associated with failing. The result of training is a model: a stored set of learned patterns.

To find out whether the model is any good, developers keep some examples aside and never show them during training. This is the test set. The model predicts results for these unseen students, and its predictions are compared with the real results. Testing on unseen data matters because the goal is to predict well for new students, not to remember old ones.

Models and predictions

Once tested, the model can be used on new data. Given a current student’s attendance, assignments and continuous assessment score, it predicts “likely to pass” or “at risk”, often with a probability such as “72% likely to pass”. A prediction is an estimate based on past patterns, not a certainty. A good use of this model would be to offer early support to students it flags; a poor use would be to treat its prediction as a judgement about a student’s ability.

Overfitting and underfitting

Two common problems show why testing matters. A model that overfits has memorised its training examples, including their random quirks, instead of learning general patterns. It scores very well on the training data but poorly on new data, like a student who memorises past-question answers word for word and fails when the questions are rephrased. A model that underfits is too simple to capture the real patterns, such as a model that predicts from attendance alone and ignores everything else. The aim is a model that generalises: one that performs well on data it has never seen.
3.4:
Supervised learning

In supervised learning, the system learns from examples that include the correct answer (labels). It comes in two main forms. Classification predicts a category: spam or not spam, pass or fail, which disease a crop leaf shows. Regression predicts a number: a house price, tomorrow’s temperature, a student’s likely examination score. Supervised learning is the most widely used type, but it needs large amounts of labelled data, and labelling is often slow and expensive human work.

Unsupervised learning

In unsupervised learning, the data has no labels. The system looks for structure on its own, most often by clustering, which means grouping similar examples together. A university could cluster students by their patterns of study activity on a learning platform and discover groups such as “steady weekly users”, “last-minute users” and “rarely active”. No one told the system these groups existed; people then interpret what the groups mean and whether they are useful.

Reinforcement learning

In reinforcement learning, a system learns by trial and error. It takes actions in an environment and receives rewards for good outcomes and penalties for bad ones, gradually learning which actions lead to the most reward. Reinforcement learning has been used to master games such as Go and to train robots. A version of it, using human feedback as the reward, is also used to make chat assistants more helpful (see 4.2).

3.5:
The neuron analogy

A neural network is a type of machine learning model loosely inspired by the brain. It is built from simple units called artificial neurons. Each neuron receives several numbers as inputs, multiplies each by a weight that reflects how important that input is, adds the results together, and passes on a signal to the next neurons. The analogy with the brain is loose: artificial neurons are simple calculations, and neural networks do not work the way brains do.

Layers and depth

Text version of Figure 3.2
  • Input layer: Attendance, Assignments, CA score
  • Hidden layers: two layers of four neurons each; every neuron is connected to every neuron in the next layer
  • Output layer: Likely to pass, At risk

The highlighted path runs from Attendance through the hidden layers to “At risk”.

Neurons are arranged in layers. The input layer receives the data, such as the pixels of an image. One or more hidden layers transform it step by step. The output layer produces the result, such as “cat” or “dog”. During training, the network compares its output with the correct answer and adjusts its weights slightly to reduce the error, repeating this millions of times.

Deep learning simply means using neural networks with many hidden layers. Depth allows a network to build up understanding in stages. In an image network, early layers tend to detect simple features such as edges; middle layers combine them into shapes such as eyes or wheels; later layers recognise whole objects. Modern networks can contain billions of weights.

What deep learning made possible

Deep learning drove most of AI’s visible progress in the past decade: accurate image recognition (face unlock, medical image analysis, crop disease detection), reliable speech recognition (voice typing and voice assistants), much better machine translation, and finally the large language models and image generators of generative AI, the subject of the next module.

Key idea

Machine learning finds patterns in examples. Its predictions are only as good as the data it learned from, and they are estimates, not certainties.
4.1:
Generating versus classifying

Most earlier AI systems classified or predicted: they sorted an email into spam or not spam, or estimated a price. Generative AI creates new content that did not exist before: a paragraph, an image, a melody, a piece of code. It does this by learning the patterns in huge collections of existing content and producing new content that follows those patterns.

4.2:
Tokens

A large language model (LLM) does not read words the way people do. It breaks text into tokens: common words, parts of words, punctuation marks and spaces. “Teaching” might be one token; a less common word such as “photosynthesis” might be split into several. As a rough guide, 100 tokens is about 75 English words. Tokens matter to users because tools limit how many tokens they can handle at once, and some charge by the token.

Next-token prediction

At its core, an LLM does one thing: given a sequence of tokens, it predicts which token is most likely to come next. It then adds that token to the sequence and predicts the next one, and the next, building a response one piece at a time.

The model does not look up an answer in a database. It produces the continuation that best fits the patterns it learned from its training text. Because it usually samples among likely tokens rather than always choosing the single most likely one, asking the same question twice can produce different answers. This mechanism explains both the model’s strength, which is fluent and flexible language on almost any topic, and its central weakness: a plausible continuation is not necessarily a true one.

Training stages

Pre-training is where the model learns language and general knowledge. It reads an enormous amount of text, from websites, books, articles and code, and repeatedly practises predicting the next token. Fine-tuning then trains it on carefully prepared examples of good responses, so that it follows instructions and answers questions rather than simply continuing text. Finally, learning from human feedback uses people’s ratings of different responses to reward the kinds of answers people find helpful, honest and safe. The result is an assistant, but one whose knowledge and habits all trace back to its training data.

Context windows

The context window is the amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can take into account at one time. It includes your prompt, any documents you paste or upload, and the conversation so far. Modern context windows are large, often enough for a whole book, but in very long conversations earlier details may be handled less reliably. Starting a fresh conversation for a new task is often better than continuing a very long one.

Knowledge cutoffs and web access

A model’s built-in knowledge stops at its knowledge cutoff, the point at which its training data was collected. It knows nothing about later events unless the tool can search the web and add the results to its context. When a tool searches, its answer is only as reliable as the pages it found and how well it summarised them. For recent events, prices, regulations and anything local, check whether the tool searched and what sources it used.
4.3:
Diffusion models

Most image generators use diffusion models. During training, the model is shown millions of images paired with descriptions. Each image is gradually covered with random visual “noise” until nothing recognisable remains, and the model learns to reverse the process step by step. To generate a new image, it starts from pure noise and removes it gradually, guided by your text description, until an image matching the description appears.

Text-to-image prompts

Image prompts work best when they describe three things: the subject (what is in the image), the style (photograph, watercolour, flat illustration, diagram) and the composition (viewpoint, setting, lighting, colour).

Example prompt

A flat, colourful illustration of a Nigerian secondary school classroom. A female teacher points to a diagram of the water cycle on a whiteboard while students in green uniforms take notes. Bright daylight from open windows, simple shapes, suitable for a children’s textbook.

Image generators still make characteristic mistakes: distorted hands, garbled text on signs and boards, wrong numbers of objects, and scenes that default to non-African settings, people and clothing unless you specify otherwise.

Audio and video generation

Similar techniques now generate speech, music and video. Text-to-speech tools can read materials aloud in natural voices, which is useful for accessibility and language practice. Voice cloning can imitate a real person’s voice from a short recording, and video tools can produce realistic clips of events that never happened. These abilities have creative uses, but they also enable fraud and misinformation, discussed in Module 10.

4.5:
Hallucination

A hallucination is output that is fluent and confident but false: an invented fact, statistic, quotation, event or reference. Hallucinations follow directly from next-token prediction. The model produces what a plausible answer would look like, and when it lacks reliable information, a plausible-looking fabrication is often what results. Fabricated academic references are a well-known example:

Example

Asked for sources on mother-tongue instruction in Nigerian primary schools, an assistant lists: “Adeyemi, B. & Okafor, C. (2019). Language of instruction and learning outcomes in South-West Nigeria. Journal of African Educational Research, 14(2), 45–61.” Every part looks correct: realistic names, a plausible title and journal, volume and page numbers. The article does not exist.

Hallucinations are reduced when a tool searches the web or works from documents you provide, but they are not eliminated. Checking methods are covered in Module 7.

Bias and representation

Models learn from their training data, and most of that data is in English and comes from North America and Europe. As a result, AI tools may know less about Nigerian contexts, perform worse in Nigerian languages, reflect stereotypes present in their data, and treat other societies’ norms as the default. Module 10 examines bias in detail.

Outdated or missing knowledge

Because of knowledge cutoffs, models may present outdated information as current: old fees, previous office holders, superseded regulations. Local information, such as a university’s own regulations, a state’s policies or a recent local event, may be missing entirely, and the model may fill the gap with a guess.

Inconsistency

The same question can produce different answers, and a slight change of wording can change the conclusion. Consistency is therefore not a reliable sign of accuracy, and inconsistency is a signal to check.

Over-reliance

The most personal risk is over-reliance. Students who let AI do their thinking, rather than support it, may produce acceptable work while failing to develop the skills the work was meant to build: writing, reasoning, calculating and remembering. Over time they also lose the ability to judge AI output, because judging requires knowledge of the subject.

5.1:
Prompts as instructions

A prompt is the input you give an AI tool: a question, an instruction, pasted material, or all three. Because a language model generates the most likely continuation of its input (see 4.2), everything in the prompt shapes the response. A prompt that says only “Write about climate change” leaves the model to guess the audience, purpose, length, level and format, and it will fall back on the most generic answer. A prompt that specifies these things steers it towards what you actually need.

VagueSpecific
Write about climate change.Write a 150-word explanation of how climate change affects farming in northern Nigeria, for JSS 2 students. Use simple language, one local example, and end with a question for class discussion.

Prompting as a skill

Prompt engineering sounds technical, but at this level it is a communication skill: giving clear instructions to a capable assistant who knows nothing about your situation. The same qualities that make instructions clear to a person, namely clarity, relevant context and a definite request, make them clear to AI. The difference is that AI never asks for clarification unless you invite it to, so the prompt must carry the context a person would ask about.
5.2:
Effective prompts usually contain some or all of five components:

ComponentWhat it doesExample wording
RoleSets the expertise and perspective the AI should adopt“Act as an experienced primary school mathematics teacher.”
TaskStates exactly what to do, with a clear action verb“Explain”, “summarise”, “compare”, “draft”, “list”, “critique”
ContextGives the audience, purpose and background“For Primary 5 pupils who struggle with fractions, as a lesson starter.”
FormatSpecifies the shape of the output“A table with three columns”; “under 200 words”; “five bullet points”
ConstraintsSets limits on tone, level, content or approach“Use Nigerian examples. Avoid technical terms. Do not give the answers.”

Here is a complete prompt with each component marked:

ComponentPrompt text
RoleYou are an experienced secondary school biology teacher.
TaskCreate five multiple-choice questions on photosynthesis
Contextfor SS 1 students revising for a class test. They have covered the inputs, outputs and the role of chlorophyll.
FormatGive four options per question, mark the correct answer, and add a one-sentence explanation for each.
ConstraintsUse simple language, include one question that applies the idea to a Nigerian crop, and avoid “all of the above”.

Not every prompt needs all five components. A quick factual question needs only a task. But when a response disappoints, a missing component, most often context or format, is usually the reason.
5.3:
Zero-shot and few-shot prompting

A zero-shot prompt asks for a task without giving examples. It works well for common tasks. A few-shot prompt includes one or more examples of what you want, so the AI can copy the pattern. Few-shot prompting is especially useful when you want a particular style or format that is hard to describe.

Few-shot prompt

Write vocabulary cards in this format.
Word: evaporate | Meaning: to change from liquid to gas | Example: Water in the pot evaporated as it boiled.
Now write cards in the same format for: condense, precipitate, absorb.

Step-by-step prompting

For problems that involve several steps, such as calculations, reasoning or planning, asking the AI to work step by step or to show its working tends to improve accuracy and, just as important, lets you check each step. Many current tools reason through problems automatically, but asking for visible steps still helps you see where an error occurs.

Example prompt

A trader buys 40 crates of tomatoes at ₦18,500 each and sells 35 crates at ₦24,000 each; the rest spoil. Work out her profit or loss step by step, showing each calculation.

Providing source material

One of the most effective techniques is to give the AI the material to work from: your lecture notes, a reading, a policy document. Then instruct it to base its answer only on that material. This is called grounding. It makes answers more relevant to your course and reduces hallucination, although it does not remove the need to check.

Example prompt

Using only the lecture notes below, list the four stages of cognitive development with the age range and one key feature of each. If something is not in the notes, say so rather than adding it. [paste notes]

Asking the AI to ask you questions

When you are unsure what information the AI needs, ask it to interview you first. This is useful for complex tasks such as planning a project or drafting a proposal.

Example prompt

I need to plan a 40-minute lesson on reading comprehension. Before you write anything, ask me up to five questions about my class and goals. Then write the plan based on my answers.
5.4:
Reading output critically

The first response is a starting point, not a finished product. Read it with three questions in mind: Is it accurate? Is it relevant to my purpose and audience? What is missing? Your answers tell you what to ask for next.

Follow-up prompts

Text version of Figure 5.1
  1. Prompt: ask clearly
  2. Read: check critically
  3. Refine: follow up

Each cycle leads to better output.

Follow-up prompts can narrow (“Focus only on the second point”), expand (“Add an example for each stage”), adjust (“Make the language simpler; the readers are JSS 1 students”), restructure (“Put this in a table”) or correct (“The date in paragraph 2 is wrong; it was 1960”). A short exchange shows how quickly output improves:

You: Give me an outline for a class debate on whether secondary school students should use AI for homework.

AI: [A general outline with arguments for and against, and a suggested format.]

You: Good. Make it suitable for SS 2 students, add three arguments on each side with a Nigerian example for each, and include rules for timing.

AI: [A revised outline with local examples and timings.]

You: Now add a one-page guide for the student chairperson, in simple language.

Each turn builds on the last. It is usually faster to refine in a few steps than to write one enormous prompt at the start.

Building a personal prompt library

When a prompt works well, save it. Keep a simple document or note of prompts you reuse, such as “explain a concept at three levels” or “turn notes into practice questions”, with blanks for the parts that change. Over a semester, a prompt library saves a great deal of time and becomes a record of your skill, useful for the portfolio in Module 14.
5.5:
MistakeWhat goes wrongFix
Vague request“Write about education” produces a generic essay that suits no oneState the specific task, audience and purpose
Overloaded promptTen tasks in one prompt; some are done badly or skippedBreak the work into steps and do them in sequence
Missing audience or purposeOutput pitched at the wrong level or in the wrong toneSay who it is for and what it will be used for
No formatA long block of text when you needed a table or listSpecify length and structure
Accepting the first answerErrors and generic content pass straight into your workRead critically, refine, and verify key facts

One misconception is worth correcting directly: longer prompts are not always better. A prompt should contain everything the AI needs and nothing that distracts it. Five precise sentences usually outperform two paragraphs of loosely related background.

Key idea

Say who it is for, what you need, and what shape it should take. Then read, refine and check.
6.1:
Built-in AI assistants

Major office suites now include AI assistants. Microsoft 365 offers Copilot in Word, PowerPoint and Excel; Google Workspace offers Gemini in Docs, Slides and Sheets; design tools such as Canva include AI features for text and images. These assistants work inside your document: they can draft a section, rewrite a paragraph, suggest slide designs or explain a formula without you leaving the file. Many of these features require a paid subscription or an institutional licence, and what is included changes frequently.

Standalone assistants

A free chat assistant used alongside your office tools can do most of the same work. You paste in text, ask for a draft or an edit, and copy the result back. This approach is slightly slower but works with any software, including free options such as Google Docs, LibreOffice and the free mobile versions of Microsoft apps.

Access realities

Many students do most of their work on a phone, with limited and costly data and unreliable power. Plan for this. Draft and edit text in short sessions, keep prompts and outputs in a notes app so work is not lost, use offline-capable apps for writing and let AI assist when you are connected, and save work to cloud storage whenever you have a connection. A phone is enough for most of the tasks in this module; a laptop helps most with spreadsheets and slide design.
6.2:
Drafting

AI is effective at overcoming the blank page. It can produce outlines for reports and essays, first drafts of formal letters, templates for lesson notes and structures for proposals. The more context you give, the more useful the draft.

Example prompt

Draft a formal letter from the Class Representative of 100 Level Educational Technology to the Head of Department, requesting an extra tutorial session before the AIIE 111 examination. Give two reasons, propose two possible dates, and keep it under 200 words in a polite, formal tone.

For academic assignments, the rules of your course decide whether AI drafting is allowed at all (see Module 11). Where it is allowed, an outline or a structure is usually a better use of AI than full paragraphs, because the thinking and writing remain yours.

Editing

AI is often most valuable as an editor of your own writing. It can correct grammar and spelling, improve clarity, adjust tone, shorten long passages and point out unclear arguments.

OriginalEdited with AI
The use of technology in the classroom is something that is very important in this present time because students of nowadays are using phones and computers for everything and so teachers should also be using it in teaching them so that they will be interested.Technology matters in today’s classrooms. Students already use phones and computers in almost every part of their lives, so teachers who bring technology into lessons can make learning more engaging and relevant.

A helpful editing prompt asks for explanations as well as changes, so that you learn: “Improve the clarity of this paragraph and list the three most important changes you made and why.”

Formatting and structure

AI can reorganise material: turning notes into headed sections, pulling key points into a summary, converting a list into a table, or suggesting a logical order for a report. This is useful for long documents such as project reports and teaching-practice files.

Keeping your voice

AI-drafted text tends to sound generic and polished in the same way: similar phrases, similar structure, few specific details. Readers, including lecturers, increasingly recognise it. Use AI as an editor, not an author: write your own draft, ask AI to improve it, then accept only the changes that make it clearer while still sounding like you. Add the specific examples, experiences and judgements that only you can provide.
6.3:
Planning a presentation

Good presentations start with three decisions: who the audience is, what single message they should leave with, and what structure will get them there. AI can help you think these through.

Example prompt

I have 10 minutes to present to my classmates on “How mobile phones can support learning in rural schools”. Suggest a clear main message and a structure of six to eight slides, with the purpose of each slide in one line.

Generating slide content

Once you have a structure, AI can draft brief slide text and speaker notes, the fuller explanation you say aloud while the slide shows only key points. Some tools, including Copilot, Gemini, Canva and Gamma, can generate a complete draft deck from a prompt or a document. These drafts save time on layout, but their content needs the same checking as any AI text, and their images may be generic or inaccurate.

Design principles

AI drafts often put too much text on each slide. The most important principle is that slides support the speaker; they do not replace them.

Text version of Figure 6.1
Before: text-heavyAfter: one idea, visual
Benefits of Mobile Learning
Eight long lines of small text fill the slide.		Phones put practice in every pocket
A phone image beside three short points: Daily quizzes · Offline reading · Peer groups
  • Less text: one idea per slide, a short headline that states the point, and a few words rather than paragraphs.
  • Visuals: a relevant image, diagram or chart communicates faster than a list.
  • Consistency: the same fonts, colours and layout throughout.
  • Readability: large text and strong contrast, since slides are often projected in bright rooms.

Checking AI slides

Before presenting, check every fact, figure and date; remove content you cannot explain; replace generic images with relevant ones; and make sure images and text you use are properly credited and permitted (see Module 11).
6.4:
Spreadsheet basics

A spreadsheet is a grid of cells, each identified by its column letter and row number (B2 is column B, row 2). Cells hold text, numbers or formulas, which begin with “=” and calculate a result from other cells. When the numbers change, the results update automatically. Spreadsheets are used for class records, budgets, survey results and simple data analysis.

AI for formulas

Formulas are where AI helps most. You can describe what you want in plain language and ask for the formula, or paste a formula you do not understand and ask for an explanation. Common functions include:

In my spreadsheet, column D has total scores out of 100 in rows 2 to 61. Write a formula for column E that gives the grade: A for 70 and above, B for 60–69, C for 50–59, D for 45–49, E for 40–44, and F below 40. Explain how the formula works.

Organising and cleaning data

Real data is often messy: names typed differently, numbers stored as text, blank rows, duplicates. AI can suggest how to clean it, for example with functions that remove extra spaces or split full names into first and last names, and can explain how to sort, filter and remove duplicates. Always keep a copy of the original data before cleaning.

Charts and simple analysis

AI can recommend the right chart for your purpose and describe patterns in data you paste. As a general guide, use a bar chart to compare categories, a line chart to show change over time, and a pie chart only for a few parts of a whole. If you ask AI to describe trends, check its statements against the numbers; AI often misreads or miscalculates figures in pasted tables.

Verifying results

A formula that runs without an error message is not necessarily correct. AI-written formulas commonly contain the wrong cell range, the wrong comparison (> instead of >=) or a reference that shifts incorrectly when copied down. Test every formula on a few rows you can calculate by hand, including edge cases such as a score of exactly 40 or exactly 70, before trusting it on a whole class.
6.5:
Email and communication

AI can draft emails and messages, adjust tone (“make this more polite”, “make this firmer”), summarise long email threads and suggest replies. For formal messages to lecturers, employers or officials, a quick AI edit can make communication clearer and more professional. Always read before sending, check names, dates and facts, and make sure the message says what you mean.

Planning and organisation

AI can turn a list of tasks into a prioritised plan, draft a weekly study timetable around your lectures and commitments, produce an agenda for a group meeting, and turn rough meeting notes into clear action points with names and deadlines. These small uses add up to significant time saved over a semester.

Knowing when not to use AI

AI is not always the efficient choice. Skip it when:

  • Checking would take longer than doing: a two-line message or a simple calculation is faster to do yourself.
  • Accuracy is critical and hard to check: official figures, legal wording, medical information.
  • The task is the learning: an assignment designed to build your writing or reasoning.
  • The task is personal: a condolence message or a personal apology should sound like you.
  • The material is confidential: other people’s personal data or restricted documents (see Module 12).

Key idea

Let AI draft, edit and calculate; you decide, check and sign your name to the result.
7.1:
Explanations at different levels

When a textbook explanation does not make sense, AI can explain the same idea in a different way, at a simpler level, or from a different starting point. You can ask for an explanation “for someone new to the subject”, “using an everyday Nigerian example” or “in three levels, from basic to advanced”. Seeing an idea explained several ways often makes it click.

Example prompt

Explain the difference between validity and reliability in educational assessment at three levels: first in one simple sentence, then in a short paragraph with an example from a school test, then in more technical terms as a textbook would. Use the same example throughout.

Worked examples and analogies

AI can produce worked examples, step-by-step solutions to problems like the ones you are studying, and analogies that connect new ideas to familiar ones. Worked examples are particularly helpful in mathematics, statistics, the sciences and accounting. Check each step: AI can make calculation errors, and a wrong worked example teaches the wrong method.

AI as a tutor

A good human tutor does not simply give answers; they ask questions that make you think. You can ask AI to tutor you the same way:

Example prompt

I am studying Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Act as a tutor. Do not explain it to me directly. Ask me one question at a time to check and deepen my understanding, tell me whether each answer is right, and give a hint if I get stuck.

This takes more effort than reading an explanation, and that is the point. Understanding an explanation feels like learning, but being able to answer questions about it is the real test.
7.2:
Research on learning consistently finds that two techniques are among the most effective: retrieval practice, which means testing yourself by recalling information from memory, and spacing, which means spreading study sessions out over time rather than cramming. Both feel harder than re-reading and highlighting, which is why students tend to avoid them, yet both produce much longer-lasting learning. AI makes both far easier to apply.

Retrieval practice with AI quizzes

AI can turn any notes into practice questions in seconds. Answer them without looking at your notes, then check.

Example prompt

From my notes below, create ten questions that test understanding, not just memory: four short-answer, four multiple-choice and two that ask me to apply an idea to a classroom situation. Put the answers at the end, separately. [paste notes]

Flashcards and spaced review

AI can also turn notes into flashcards: a question or term on the front, the answer on the back. Review them over increasing intervals, for example after one day, three days, a week and two weeks, spending more time on cards you get wrong. Flashcard apps such as Anki schedule this automatically; paper cards in labelled piles work just as well.

Summaries and study guides

AI can summarise readings and turn scattered notes into organised study guides with key terms, main ideas and examples. Always check a summary against your notes or the original: AI summaries can leave out important points, change the meaning of cautious statements, or add information that was not in the source.

Revision timetables

Give AI your examination dates, the topics for each course, your other commitments and the time you realistically have, and ask for a revision timetable that spaces topics out and includes self-testing. Then review it critically. AI timetables are often too full, with no rest time; adjust them until they are realistic, because a plan you cannot follow is worse than a modest one you can.
7.3:
Finding sources

General chat assistants are not reliable for finding academic sources on their own, because they may fabricate references. Better tools for finding real sources include:

ToolWhat it does
Google ScholarSearches academic articles, books and theses; shows how often each is cited
University library databasesJournals and e-books your institution subscribes to; ask the library about access
AI research toolsTools such as Semantic Scholar, Elicit, Consensus and Perplexity search real academic papers and summarise them, with links to the sources
African sourcesAfrican Journals Online (AJOL) and university repositories hold research on African and Nigerian topics that global tools may miss

Research tools that link to real papers are safer than general assistants, but their summaries can still be inaccurate. Always open the source.

Reading and summarising papers

Academic papers can be difficult to read. AI can help you understand a paper you have found: explaining technical terms, summarising the research question, method, findings and limitations, and relating it to your topic. Upload or paste the paper itself rather than asking about it by title, so the AI works from the actual text. Read the abstract, introduction and conclusion yourself; you are responsible for what you cite.

Organising literature

Once you have several sources, AI can help you organise them into themes, identify where authors agree and disagree, and build a comparison table (author, year, context, method, key finding). This structure is the foundation of a literature review. The judgements about which sources matter and what they mean together remain yours.

Research questions

Many student projects struggle because the topic is too broad. AI can help you narrow it. “Technology in education” becomes “the use of mobile phones for homework among JSS students in Ijebu-Ode”, which becomes a question that can actually be answered: “How do JSS 3 students in two Ijebu-Ode schools use mobile phones to complete homework?” Ask AI to suggest narrower versions of your topic and to identify what data each question would need.
7.4:
Fabricated references

As explained in Module 4, AI can generate references that look completely genuine but do not exist, because it produces what a reference looks like. Some fabricated references mix real and invented details: a real author with an invented title, or a real journal with an invented article. Never cite a source you have not found and opened yourself.

StepWhat to doIf it fails
1. Searchtitle in Google Scholar or the libraryNot found
2. Matchauthors, year, journal and pagesNot found
3. Openand read the relevant partCan’t access
