All four steps pass → Cite. Any failure: do not cite it. Find a real source for the claim.

A reference passes only when you have found the actual source and confirmed that it says what you are citing it for. The last step matters because AI sometimes cites a real source for a claim the source does not make.

Cross-checking claims

For factual claims, such as statistics, dates, definitions, laws and policies, check the primary source where possible: the original report, the official statistics agency, the legislation itself, the organisation’s own website. For Nigerian data, relevant primary sources include the National Bureau of Statistics, government ministries and agencies, and official publications of bodies such as the Universal Basic Education Commission. Where sources disagree, report the disagreement rather than choosing the most convenient figure.

Evaluating sources

Whether a source comes from AI or your own search, evaluate it on three criteria:

CriterionQuestions to ask
AuthorityWho wrote it? What are their qualifications? Is it peer-reviewed or from a reputable organisation?
CurrencyWhen was it published? Is the information still current for your topic?
RelevanceDoes it address your question and context? Is it about a similar population or setting?

Local context

Global AI tools know most about the countries that produce most of their training data. For Nigerian topics, AI may fill gaps with information from other countries, present outdated policies as current, or invent local details. Look deliberately for Nigerian and African sources, and treat AI claims about local facts with particular caution.
7.5:
Learning versus outsourcing

The key question is whether AI is doing the thinking with you or for you. AI supports learning when it explains, questions, gives feedback and helps you practise. It undermines learning when it produces the work the task was designed to make you do, such as writing the essay, solving the problems or summarising the reading you were meant to understand.

Supports learningReplaces learning
Explaining a concept you are stuck onWriting your assignment answer
Quizzing you on your notesAnswering the quiz for you
Giving feedback on your draftProducing the draft
Checking your worked solutionSolving the problem set

Following course and institutional rules

Rules on AI use differ between institutions, departments, courses and even individual assignments. Some tasks allow AI freely, some allow it for specific purposes with acknowledgement, and some prohibit it. Find out the rules for each course, and when they are unclear, ask your lecturer before you use AI, not after. Module 11 covers academic integrity in detail.

Recording AI use

Keep a simple record of significant AI use: the date, the tool, the prompts you used, what you did with the output and how you checked it. A prompt log takes a few minutes to maintain. It protects you if your work is questioned, makes it easy to write an AI-use statement, and provides evidence for your portfolio in Module 14.

Key idea

Use AI to make yourself think harder, not less. Never cite a source you have not opened.
8.1:
Definitions

Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying an opportunity and taking initiative to create value from it, usually by organising resources and accepting some risk. The value may be financial profit, but it may also be social benefit, better services or new knowledge. An entrepreneur is someone who does this. The definition is deliberately broad: a student who organises a paid tutoring service, a teacher who designs a better way to run parent meetings and a founder who builds a national company are all acting entrepreneurially.

Types of entrepreneurship

TypeMain aimExample
Business entrepreneurshipProfit from products or servicesA printing and typing business near campus
Social entrepreneurshipSolving a social problem, often with a sustainable income modelA low-cost reading programme for out-of-school children
IntrapreneurshipInnovating inside an existing organisationA teacher who introduces a new peer-tutoring system in their school
EdupreneurshipCreating value in educationExamination-preparation content, learning materials, tutoring platforms

Edupreneurship and intrapreneurship are particularly relevant for students preparing for careers in education. Many of the most useful innovations in schools come from teachers who notice a problem and try a better approach.

Entrepreneurship in Nigeria

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) form the great majority of businesses in Nigeria and provide a large share of employment. Much economic activity takes place in the informal sector: traders, artisans and service providers operating without formal registration. With a young and fast-growing population and more graduates than formal jobs, youth enterprise is widely promoted by government, universities and development organisations. Many Nigerian universities include entrepreneurship in the curriculum for this reason. Entrepreneurship is not a substitute for employment for everyone, but the mindset it builds is valuable in any career.
8.2:
Core traits

An entrepreneurial mindset is a set of attitudes and habits that help people recognise and act on opportunities. It is not a fixed personality type. Its core traits include:

TraitWhat it looks like in practice
InitiativeActing on a problem rather than waiting for someone else to solve it
ResilienceContinuing after setbacks and rejections
CreativitySeeing new combinations and approaches
Calculated risk-takingAccepting uncertainty while limiting what can be lost
Customer focusStarting from what people need, not from what you want to sell

Growth mindset

A growth mindset is the belief that abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and feedback. It is associated with the psychologist Carol Dweck. For entrepreneurs, it means treating failure as information: an idea that does not work shows what customers do not want, which is valuable to know. Most successful ventures change significantly from their first idea because their founders learned from what went wrong.

Resourcefulness

Many people believe they cannot start anything without capital. Entrepreneurial thinking starts instead with what you already have: your skills, knowledge, network, time and the tools available to you. A student with a phone, AI tools and good subject knowledge already has the resources to create study materials, offer tutoring or produce educational content. Starting small and growing from results is safer than borrowing to start big.
8.3:
Sources of opportunity

An opportunity is a situation in which a need can be met in a way that creates value. Opportunities come from several sources:

Text version of Figure 8.1
  • Problems: repeated frustrations
  • Changes: new policies, habits, events
  • Gaps: needs others ignore
  • New technology: what is now possible or cheap

All four lead to an opportunity.

  • Problems: frustrations people experience repeatedly, such as long queues, missing information or unreliable services.
  • Changes: new policies, demographic shifts, new habits, or events that create new needs.
  • Gaps: needs that existing products ignore, often because a group is too small, too poor or too remote for large companies.
  • New technology: tools that make something possible or cheap that was previously impossible or expensive.

Opportunity recognition

Opportunity recognition works in three steps: noticing problems and changes (keeping a record of frustrations you and others experience helps); connecting them to things you know or can do; and evaluating whether the resulting idea is worth pursuing (see 8.4). People with knowledge of a particular field, such as education, often see opportunities that outsiders miss, because they understand the problems from the inside.

AI-enabled opportunities

AI has lowered the cost of producing content, analysing information and offering services, creating new opportunities at student scale:

TypeExamples at student scale
ServicesHelping small businesses write product descriptions, social media posts or simple websites; translation and transcription services, with human checking
ContentEducational videos, revision guides and practice question banks for specific examinations or subjects
ToolsSimple chatbots or templates built with no-code tools for a specific need, such as answering common questions for a school
EducationTraining teachers, parents or small business owners to use AI tools effectively

Because these opportunities are open to everyone with the same tools, the advantage goes to those who combine AI with something harder to copy: subject expertise, local knowledge, trust, quality control or a specific community they understand well.
8.4:
Simple screening

Most ideas are not worth pursuing, and finding this out early is a success, not a failure. Four questions provide a quick screen:

Four-question opportunity screen

  • Need: Is this a real, frequent or serious problem for a specific group of people? How do you know?
  • Market: How many people have this problem, and would they pay, or act, to solve it? What do they use now?
  • Feasibility: Can you actually deliver a solution with available skills and technology?
  • Resources: What would it cost in money, time and effort to start, and can you start small?

An idea that fails on need should usually be dropped, however clever the solution. An idea that fails on resources can often be redesigned to start smaller.

Value proposition basics

A value proposition states clearly who you help, with what problem, and how your solution is better than the alternatives. A simple template is: “For [specific group] who [problem], our [solution] provides [main benefit], unlike [current alternative].” For example: “For SS 3 students in Ogun State preparing for WAEC Biology, our weekly WhatsApp quiz service provides short daily practice with explained answers, unlike thick past-question books with no explanations.”

Using AI to explore ideas

AI can help at each step: generating ideas from a problem, listing possible customer groups, identifying competitors and risks, and drafting a value proposition. Its knowledge of local markets is limited and sometimes wrong, so treat its market claims as questions to investigate rather than findings.

Example prompt

I am a 100-level education student in Ogun State. I want to start a small, low-cost business using my knowledge of mathematics and free AI tools. Suggest five ideas. For each, give the target customers, what they currently use instead, the main risk, and how I could test demand in two weeks for under ₦10,000.
8.5:
Nigerian and African technology ventures

Several well-known Nigerian ventures illustrate the ideas above. Paystack began by solving a specific problem, how small online businesses could accept card payments easily, and was acquired by the US company Stripe in 2020. uLesson identified the gap in affordable, curriculum-aligned video lessons for secondary students and delivered them on devices and in formats suited to students with limited data. Hello Tractor connected smallholder farmers who could not afford tractors with tractor owners who had idle machines. In each case the starting point was a clearly understood problem for a specific group, not a technology looking for a use. (Company details change; check current information before quoting them.)

Student-scale ventures

Most entrepreneurship starts far smaller. Consider three student-scale examples:

VentureProblemWhy it can work
Subject tutoring for secondary studentsParents want help for children in specific subjects before examinationsUses subject knowledge; low start-up cost; AI helps prepare materials
Social media content for local shopsSmall businesses lack time and skill for regular postsUses AI for drafts and images; human judgement ensures quality and local relevance
Typing, formatting and project supportStudents and staff need documents formatted to institutional standardsUses office and AI skills; steady demand around deadlines (within academic integrity rules)

Key idea

Start from a real problem for specific people, begin with what you have, and test before you invest.
9.1:
Why solutions fail

People often begin with a solution they find exciting, such as an app, a device or a website, and then look for a problem it could solve. This solution-first thinking is the most common reason new ideas fail. The solution may be well made, but if the problem is minor, rare or already solved well enough, no one will use it. A student who builds a campus timetable app may discover that everyone already uses the departmental WhatsApp group and sees no reason to switch.

Problem-first thinking reverses the order. It starts by understanding a problem deeply, including who has it, when, how often, how they cope now and why current solutions fall short, and only then considers solutions.

Problems worth solving

Not every problem is worth solving. Three questions help:

QuestionWhy it matters
How often does it happen?Frequent problems create steady demand; rare ones are easily tolerated
How severe is it?Serious problems, costing money, time, health or opportunity, motivate people to change
Will people pay or act to solve it?If people complain but will not spend money, time or effort on a solution, it is not yet an opportunity

A useful sign of a real problem is that people are already trying to solve it with workarounds: improvised, inconvenient methods such as photocopying a classmate’s notes, paying someone to queue, or keeping records in several notebooks.
9.2:
Observation

Observation means watching what people actually do in the real setting where the problem occurs. It is powerful because people’s behaviour often differs from their descriptions of it. Students may say they study every evening, but observing the library shows when it is actually full. Note what people do, where they struggle, what workarounds they use and what they seem to find frustrating.

Interviews

Interviews reveal why people do what they do. Good needs-finding interviews ask about past behaviour and specific experiences, not opinions about imaginary products. The most common mistake is the leading question, which suggests the answer the interviewer wants:

Leading questionOpen question
Don’t you think a revision app would help you?Tell me about the last time you prepared for an examination. What did you do?
Would you pay ₦500 for this service?What have you spent money or time on to help with your studies this semester?
Isn’t it frustrating that lecture notes are hard to get?How do you get notes when you miss a lecture?

Listen more than you talk. Ask “why?” and “can you tell me more about that?” Record specific stories and exact words, which are more reliable than general impressions.

Surveys

Surveys are useful for measuring how common something is across many people, once you already understand the problem through observation and interviews. They are poor at discovering problems you have not thought of. Keep surveys short, use simple and neutral wording, ask one thing per question, and test the survey on two or three people before sending it out. Free tools such as Google Forms make surveys easy to distribute through WhatsApp groups.

Secondary research

Secondary research uses information others have already collected: government statistics, research reports, news articles, and the websites and reviews of existing solutions. It tells you the size of a problem and what has already been tried, so you do not repeat known failures.
9.3:
The stages of design thinking

Design thinking is a human-centred approach to solving problems, widely used in business, education and public services. It is usually described in five stages:

Text version of Figure 9.1
  1. Empathise
  2. Define
  3. Ideate
  4. Prototype
  5. Test

Testing often sends you back to an earlier stage.

StageWhat you do
EmpathiseUnderstand the people affected, through observation and interviews
DefineState the core problem clearly from their point of view
IdeateGenerate many possible solutions before choosing
PrototypeMake quick, cheap versions of the most promising ideas
TestTry prototypes with real users and learn from their reactions

The stages form a loop rather than a straight line. Testing often reveals that the problem was defined wrongly, which sends you back to empathise or define.

Empathy maps and user personas

An empathy map organises what you learned about a user into four areas. Here is one for a first-year student at a university of education:

Says
“I don’t know which topics will come out in the exam.” “The handouts finish before I can buy them.”		Thinks
Worries about carrying over courses; unsure whether studying alone is enough.
Does
Photographs classmates’ notes; studies late at night; reads past questions a week before exams.		Feels
Anxious before examinations; overwhelmed by the number of courses; relieved when working in a group.

A user persona is a short, realistic profile of a typical user, based on your research: for example, “Tolu, 19, 100-level Biology Education student, commutes from Ijebu-Ode, studies mainly on her phone, limited data”. Personas keep the team focused on real people rather than an imagined average user. They must be based on real research; a persona invented without talking to anyone only records your assumptions.

Writing a problem statement

A good problem statement combines three elements: the user, their need and an insight that explains why the need matters. A common formula is:

[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].

For example: “First-year students at a university of education need a way to know which topics matter most in each course, because they study reactively in the week before exams and cannot tell what to prioritise.” Notice that the statement describes the need without naming a solution. It leaves room for many possible ideas, such as study guides, peer groups, course outlines or practice quizzes.
9.4:
Drafting interview guides and surveys

AI can draft interview guides and survey questions quickly, and it can check your drafts for leading, confusing or double-barrelled questions (questions that ask two things at once).

Example prompt

I am researching how first-year students prepare for examinations. Draft eight open interview questions that ask about specific past experiences, not opinions about possible products. Then review them and flag any that are leading or ask two things at once.

Analysing responses

After interviews or surveys, AI can help you find themes: patterns that appear across many responses. Paste your notes (with names and identifying details removed; see Module 12) and ask AI to group them into themes, with example quotes for each. Check its themes against your own reading. AI may overstate a theme mentioned once, or miss something important said in an unusual way.

Limits: AI cannot replace talking to real people

AI can generate convincing “user personas” and imagined interview answers in seconds. These are not research. They reflect patterns in AI’s training data, which may not match your users, especially in a specific Nigerian context, and they cannot reveal the surprises that make real research valuable. Use AI to prepare for and analyse research, never as a substitute for it.
9.5:
Testing assumptions

Every idea rests on assumptions: that people have the problem, that they will use your solution, that they will pay. Validation means testing the riskiest assumptions first, as quickly and cheaply as possible. Useful low-cost tests include describing the idea to potential users and asking them to sign up or pre-order, running a free trial for a small group, or offering the service manually before building any technology.

Simple prototypes

A prototype is an early, rough version of a solution made to learn, not to sell. It can be a paper sketch of app screens, a mock-up made in a free design tool, a one-page flyer, a single sample lesson or a WhatsApp group run by hand. A prototype should take hours or days to make, not months. The rougher it is, the more willing people are to criticise it honestly.

Feedback and iteration

Show prototypes to real users and watch how they respond. Ask what they would change, but pay most attention to what they do: whether they sign up, use it, return to it or recommend it. Then iterate: improve the idea, or abandon it and try another. Each cycle of building, testing and learning should be small and fast.

  1. Identify the riskiest assumption behind your idea.
  2. Design the cheapest test that could prove it wrong.
  3. Run the test with real potential users.
  4. Decide: continue, change the idea, or stop.

Key idea

Understand the problem before you design the solution, and test with real people before you build.
10.1:
AI decisions affecting people

When AI recommends a song, a mistake costs little. When AI helps decide who is admitted, hired, given credit, investigated or treated, a mistake can change a life. These decisions often happen at scale, affecting thousands of people in the same way, and the people affected may not know that AI was involved or how to challenge the result. AI ethics is the study of how AI should be designed and used so that it benefits people and avoids harm.

AreaHow AI may be usedWhat could go wrong
EducationPredicting at-risk students; automated marking; detecting AI-written workWrongly labelling students; unfair marks; false accusations of cheating
EmploymentScreening CVs; analysing video interviewsRejecting qualified candidates who differ from past hires
LendingCredit scoring from phone and transaction dataExcluding people with little digital history
PolicingFacial recognition; predicting crime locationsMisidentification; over-policing particular communities

Core principles

Many governments, companies and international bodies have published AI ethics principles. Although the wording differs, most share six core principles:

PrincipleWhat it means
FairnessAI should not discriminate unjustly or produce systematically worse outcomes for particular groups.
TransparencyPeople should know when AI is being used, and decisions should be explainable in understandable terms.
AccountabilityIdentifiable people and organisations remain responsible for what AI systems do.
PrivacyPersonal data should be collected and used lawfully, minimally and securely.
SafetyAI should work reliably and be protected against misuse and harmful failure.
Human oversightPeople should be able to monitor, question and override AI decisions that affect others.

Principles can conflict. Greater transparency about how a fraud-detection system works may help fraudsters avoid it; stronger privacy may limit the data needed to check a system for fairness. Ethical judgement involves weighing such trade-courseIds, not just listing principles.

International frameworks

The most widely adopted international framework is the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, adopted by UNESCO’s member states in November 2021. It sets out values and principles including human rights and dignity, fairness and non-discrimination, transparency, and environmental sustainability, and it asks governments to put them into policy, including in education. Nigeria has also been developing its own national AI strategy, which addresses ethics alongside economic goals.
10.2:
Sources of bias

Bias in AI means systematic errors that unfairly favour or disadvantage particular groups. It rarely comes from anyone intending to discriminate. It enters at three stages:

Text version of Figure 10.1
  1. Data ⚠: groups under-represented; past unfairness recorded
  2. Design ⚠: choices of what to predict and which features to use
  3. Deployment ⚠: used in a new context; outputs trusted too much

→ Unfair outcomes

  • Data: the training data under-represents some groups or reflects past discrimination. A hiring model trained on the CVs of past successful employees learns to prefer people like them.
  • Design: choices made by developers, such as what to predict, which features to use and how to measure success, build in assumptions. Using postcode as a feature can indirectly stand in for ethnicity or income.
  • Deployment: a system is used in a context different from the one it was built for, or its outputs are trusted more than they should be.

Removing sensitive features such as gender or ethnicity from the data does not remove bias, because other features, such as name, school, location or language, can act as proxies for them.

Examples

Several well-documented cases illustrate the problem. Research published in 2018 found that commercial facial analysis systems made far more errors for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men, largely because their training data contained far fewer images of darker-skinned faces. An experimental hiring tool developed by Amazon was reported to have downgraded CVs containing the word “women’s”, because it had learned from a decade of mostly male hires; the company abandoned it. Speech recognition systems have been found to make more errors for some accents than others, disadvantaging speakers whose accents were under-represented in training.

Bias affecting Africa

For African users, bias often takes the form of under-representation. Most training data comes from other regions, so AI tools may perform worse for African faces, voices, names and languages; may know little about African history, institutions and current affairs; and may treat Western norms as universal. Nigerian languages have far less digital text than English, so AI performs worse in Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Pidgin. Ask an image generator for “a successful professional” or “a beautiful home”, and the default result often does not look Nigerian.

Recognising bias in outputs

You can check AI outputs for bias by asking: Who is shown or assumed by default? Who is missing? Would the answer change if the person described were of a different gender, ethnicity, religion or region? Does the output rely on stereotypes? A simple test is to rerun a prompt changing only one detail, such as a name or location, and compare the outputs.
10.3:
Deepfakes

A deepfake is synthetic media, meaning an image, audio clip or video generated or altered by AI, that realistically shows a person saying or doing something they never said or did. Deepfake technology is now cheap and widely available. A few seconds of recorded speech can be enough to clone a voice, and convincing fake photographs can be made from a text prompt.

AI-generated misinformation

Synthetic media and AI-generated text are used to spread misinformation (false information shared without intent to deceive) and disinformation (false information spread deliberately). Areas of particular concern include:

  • Elections: fake audio or video of candidates, and large volumes of AI-written posts that make a view appear more popular than it is.
  • Health: fabricated cures and false claims presented with a confident, scientific tone.
  • Scams: cloned voices of relatives asking for urgent money transfers; fake videos of celebrities or officials promoting investments.

Detection and verification

Detecting synthetic media by eye is becoming harder, and automated detection tools are unreliable. Verification habits matter more than spotting visual flaws:

Before you believe or share

  • Check the source: who first posted it? Is it an official account or a reputable news organisation?
  • Look for confirmation: is the same story reported by several independent, reliable sources?
  • Search the image: a reverse image search (for example Google Lens or TinEye) can show whether an image is old, altered or from a different event.
  • Be suspicious of urgency and emotion: content designed to make you angry, afraid or rushed is a warning sign.
  • Verify requests for money through a separate channel, such as calling the person on a number you already know.
10.4:
Environmental cost

Training and running large AI models requires large data centres that use substantial electricity and, for cooling, water. Estimates of AI’s total environmental footprint vary widely and change as technology changes, but the direction is clear: as AI use grows, so does its demand for energy. Responsible use includes asking whether a task needs AI at all, especially energy-intensive image and video generation.

Labour

AI systems depend on large amounts of human work that users rarely see: labelling images, rating responses and filtering harmful content from training data. Much of this work has been outsourced to lower-income countries, including in Africa. Investigations have reported low pay and difficult conditions for some of these workers, particularly those reviewing disturbing content. AI’s apparent automation often rests on human labour.

Concentration of power

Building the most capable AI models requires enormous amounts of data, computing power and money, so a small number of large companies, mostly in the United States and China, control the most advanced systems. Their decisions about what AI can do, what it refuses to do, what it costs and whose languages and values it reflects affect billions of people who have no say in them. This raises questions about digital sovereignty: how countries such as Nigeria can build their own AI capacity, protect their citizens’ data and ensure AI serves local needs.
10.5:
Personal guidelines

Responsible AI use can be summarised in four habits:

  1. Check: Verify facts, figures, references and anything important before you use or share it.
  2. Disclose: Be honest about when and how you used AI, following the rules that apply.
  3. Protect: Keep personal, confidential and other people’s data out of AI tools.
  4. Respect: Do not use AI to deceive, impersonate, harass or harm others, or to take credit for others’ work.

Human in the loop

A human in the loop means that a person reviews and takes responsibility for AI outputs before they affect anyone. The review must be real: a person who approves every AI suggestion without reading it provides no oversight. The more an output could affect someone, the more careful the human review should be. The same applies to your own use: you are the human in the loop for everything you submit, post or send.

Responsible use in teaching and learning

For students preparing to teach, responsible AI use has an extra dimension, because learners will copy the habits they see. Responsible teachers use AI to prepare and differentiate materials but check them carefully; never enter learners’ personal information into AI tools; explain clearly when learners may use AI and how to acknowledge it; design tasks that still require learners to think; and are open about their own AI use. Above all, they do not let AI make judgements about individual learners that should be made by a teacher who knows them.

Key idea

Check, disclose, protect, respect. AI can assist decisions about people, but people remain responsible for them.
11.1:
Types of intellectual property

Intellectual property (IP) refers to creations of the mind, such as writing, music, art, inventions, designs, names and symbols, that the law allows their creators to own and control. IP law aims to balance two goods: rewarding creators so that they keep creating, and allowing the public to benefit from and build on their work.

TypeWhat it protectsExampleHow long (general terms)
CopyrightOriginal creative expression: writing, music, art, films, softwareA textbook; a song; a lecture videoFor literary, musical and artistic works in Nigeria, the author’s life plus 70 years
PatentNew, useful inventionsA new water-purification deviceA limited term, typically 20 years; must be applied for
TrademarkNames, logos and signs that identify a brandA company’s name and logoCan be renewed indefinitely while in use and registered
Trade secretValuable confidential business informationA recipe; a customer listAs long as it is kept secret

Copyright is the type most relevant to students, because it covers almost everything you read, watch, copy and write. It arises automatically when an original work is created in a fixed form; no registration is needed. It protects the expression of ideas, not the ideas themselves: anyone may explain photosynthesis, but not copy another author’s explanation word for word.

Copyright in Nigeria

Copyright in Nigeria is governed by the Copyright Act 2022, which replaced the earlier Copyright Act and was signed into law in March 2023. It updated the law for the digital age: it explicitly covers digital copies and online infringement, provides for owners to require online service providers to take down or block infringing content, and extended the term of protection for literary, musical and artistic works to 70 years after the author’s death. The Nigerian Copyright Commission (NCC) is the government agency responsible for administering and enforcing copyright, including registering works (which is voluntary but helpful as evidence) and prosecuting infringement.

Fair dealing

Copyright is not absolute. The Act allows certain uses of copyright works without permission under fair dealing, including for private use, research, education, criticism, review and news reporting, provided the use is fair. Fairness depends on factors such as the purpose of the use, the nature of the work, how much is used, and whether the use harms the market for the original. Quoting a short passage from a book in an essay, with a citation, is fair dealing; photocopying an entire textbook to sell is not.
11.2:
Training data and copyright

Generative AI models are trained on vast amounts of text, images and other content, much of it protected by copyright and used without the creators’ permission. Authors, artists, news organisations and music companies have brought legal cases against AI developers, arguing that this use infringes their rights. Developers argue that training is a permitted use, similar to a person learning by reading. Courts in different countries are still deciding these questions, and the law is unsettled.

Ownership of AI output

Copyright traditionally protects works created by human authors. In several countries, including the United States, authorities have held that material generated entirely by AI, without meaningful human creative input, cannot be protected by copyright, although human selection, arrangement and modification of AI output may be. Nigerian law has not yet settled the question. For practical purposes: the more of your own creative work you put into something, the stronger your claim to it; and AI output is not “nobody’s work” that you can present as your own original writing in an academic setting.

Using AI images and text

Each AI tool has terms of service that state what you may do with its output, including whether commercial use is allowed. Read them before using AI output in a business. Be especially careful with outputs that imitate a real artist’s style, reproduce recognisable characters or logos, or show real people; these can raise copyright, trademark or personality-rights issues regardless of the tool’s terms. When using images or text created by others, including stock images found online, check the licence. Creative Commons licences, for example, allow reuse under stated conditions such as crediting the creator.
11.3:
Forms of plagiarism

Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s words, ideas or work as your own without proper acknowledgement. It is an academic offence whether or not it breaks copyright law, and whether or not it is intentional.

FormWhat it is
Direct copyingCopying text word for word without quotation marks and a citation
Paraphrase plagiarismRewording someone’s ideas closely without citing them
PatchwritingStitching together phrases from sources with small changes, so the text is neither quoted nor truly in your own words
Self-plagiarismResubmitting your own previous work for new credit without permission
CollusionSubmitting work done with others as individual work when the task was individual

AI-assisted plagiarism

Submitting text, code, images or analysis generated by AI as if you produced it yourself is a form of academic misconduct, even though no human author is being copied. The work does not represent your learning, and presenting it as yours is dishonest. Using AI to disguise copied text, for example by asking it to paraphrase a source so that plagiarism software will not detect it, is plagiarism of the original source as well.

Plagiarism detection

Plagiarism-checking software such as Turnitin compares submitted work with large databases of web pages, publications and previously submitted assignments, and highlights matching text. A similarity score is not a verdict: quotations and common phrases also match, and a lecturer must interpret the report.

Many institutions also use AI-detection tools, which estimate how likely it is that text was generated by AI. These tools are much less reliable. They produce false positives, flagging genuine human writing as AI-generated, and research has found that writing by people using English as a second language is flagged more often. They are also easy to evade. For this reason, a detector score alone should not be treated as proof of misconduct. Keeping drafts, notes and a record of your AI use (see 7.5) is your best protection if your work is ever questioned.
11.4:
Institutional and course policies

Academic integrity means honesty, fairness and responsibility in academic work. Institutions and lecturers set different rules for AI, and rules may differ between assignments in the same course. Most fall somewhere on a spectrum:

Text version of Figure 11.1
Not permittedPermitted with disclosureFreely permitted
Examinations and testsBrainstorming; outliningPractising with an AI tutor
Tasks that state “no AI”Grammar feedback on your draftSelf-quizzing on your notes

Typical examples only. The rules for each course and task decide.

If a task’s rules do not mention AI, do not assume it is allowed. Ask your lecturer. The responsibility to know the rules rests with the student.

Disclosing AI use

Where AI use is permitted, you are usually expected to disclose it. A clear AI-use statement says which tool you used, for what, and how you checked or changed the output:

Sample AI-use statement

I used ChatGPT to suggest an outline for this essay and to check the grammar of my final draft. I wrote all the paragraphs myself, changed the order of the outline, and verified every source by locating and reading it. My prompts are included in the appendix.

Citing AI

When you quote or directly use AI-generated content, cite it according to the referencing style your department requires. Referencing styles have published guidance for AI. In APA (7th edition) style, the developer is treated as the author:

OpenAI. (2026). ChatGPT [Large language model]. https://chatgpt.com

with an in-text citation such as (OpenAI, 2026), and a description of your prompt in the text. In MLA style, the prompt is described in the title position:

“Explain the difference between validity and reliability” prompt. ChatGPT, OpenAI, 12 Mar. 2026, chatgpt.com.

Include the version of the model if the tool shows it, and check your department’s current guidance, since style rules for AI are still evolving. Remember that citing AI does not make it a reliable source: for facts and claims, find and cite the original source.

Consequences of misconduct

Academic misconduct can lead to a failed assignment or course, suspension, expulsion, or, if discovered later, withdrawal of a degree. Beyond the formal penalties, misconduct means missing the learning the task was meant to provide. For future teachers, integrity carries extra weight: you will be responsible for upholding it in your own learners.
11.5:
Why we cite

Referencing serves three purposes. It gives credit to the people whose work you used. It allows readers to verify your claims by finding your sources. And it places your work within the wider scholarship on the topic, showing what you have read and where your own contribution begins.

Citation basics

Most referencing styles have two parts: an in-text citation at the point where you use a source, and a reference list at the end with full details. In APA style:

ElementExample
In-text, paraphraseRetrieval practice improves long-term retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
In-text, author named in sentenceRoediger and Karpicke (2006) found that students who tested themselves remembered more a week later than students who re-read.
Direct quotationAdd quotation marks and the page number: (Author, Year, p. X).
Reference list entryRoediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.

Use the style your department requires, consistently. AI can help format references, but it often introduces errors in details such as volume numbers, page ranges and author initials, so check each formatted reference against the source.

Reference managers

Reference managers such as Zotero (free and open source) and Mendeley (free) store your sources, capture their details from library databases and web pages, and insert correctly formatted citations and reference lists into your documents. Learning one early in your studies saves many hours during project and dissertation writing.

Key idea

Know the rules, disclose your AI use, and credit every source. If in doubt, ask before you submit.
12.1:
What personal data is

Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable living person. Some data identifies a person directly: a name, a photograph, a National Identification Number (NIN), a phone number or an email address. Other data identifies a person indirectly, when combined with other information: a matriculation number, a location history, a device identifier, or a combination such as “the only 300-level Physics Education student from Sagamu”. Data about someone’s opinions, behaviour and preferences is also personal data if it can be linked to them.

The law gives extra protection to sensitive personal data, because its misuse can cause serious harm or discrimination. Under Nigerian law this includes data about a person’s health, genetic and biometric data (such as fingerprints and facial images used for identification), race or ethnic origin, religious or similar beliefs, political opinions or affiliations, trade union membership, and sex life or sexual orientation.

Data in daily life

Nigerians share personal data constantly: registering a SIM card and linking it to a NIN, opening a bank account with a Bank Verification Number (BVN), using fintech and ride-hailing apps, signing up for social media, and completing school and university registration. Universities and schools hold contact details, results, fees, medical and disciplinary records.

Data as value

Organisations collect data because it is valuable. It helps them provide services, but also to target advertising, assess credit, predict behaviour and train AI systems. Many “free” apps are paid for with users’ data. Individuals therefore have a real interest in knowing what is collected about them and how it is used.
12.2:
Purpose and scope

The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA) was signed into law in June 2023. It provides a legal framework for protecting personal data and safeguarding the privacy of individuals in Nigeria. It applies to organisations and individuals who process personal data, whether in the public or private sector, when they are based in Nigeria, when the processing takes place in Nigeria, or when they process the data of people in Nigeria. Two roles are central: the data controller, who decides why and how personal data is processed (such as a university or a bank), and the data processor, who processes data on the controller’s behalf (such as a cloud service provider). The person the data is about is the data subject.

The Nigeria Data Protection Commission

The Act established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as the regulator. The NDPC oversees compliance, issues regulations and guidance, registers organisations that process large amounts of data, investigates complaints from data subjects and can impose penalties. In 2025 it issued the General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID), which gives detailed guidance on applying the Act.

Principles

The Act requires personal data to be processed according to a set of principles:

PrincipleWhat it requiresEveryday example
Lawfulness, fairness and transparencyProcess data on a lawful basis, fairly, and tell people what you are doingA school explains why it collects parents’ phone numbers
Purpose limitationCollect data for specified, legitimate purposes and not use it for incompatible onesNumbers collected for emergencies are not sold to advertisers
Data minimisationCollect only what is adequate, relevant and necessaryA club registration form does not ask for religion or BVN
Storage limitationKeep data no longer than necessaryOld application forms are securely destroyed after the retention period
AccuracyKeep data accurate and up to dateA student can correct a misspelled name on their record
Integrity, confidentiality and securityProtect data against unauthorised access, loss and damageResult files are password-protected and access is restricted

Controllers are also accountable: they must be able to show that they comply.

Lawful bases

Processing personal data is lawful only if it has at least one lawful basis. The Act lists six: the data subject’s consent; the performance of a contract with the data subject; compliance with a legal obligation; protecting someone’s vital interests (for example in a medical emergency); a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority; and the controller’s legitimate interests, provided these are not overridden by the data subject’s rights. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and it can be withdrawn. Processing children’s data generally requires the consent of a parent or guardian.

Data subject rights

The Act gives individuals rights over their personal data:

RightWhat it allows you to do
Information and accessKnow whether your data is being processed and obtain a copy of it
RectificationHave inaccurate or incomplete data corrected
ErasureHave data deleted in certain circumstances, for example when it is no longer needed
ObjectionObject to certain processing of your data, including for direct marketing
Withdraw consentWithdraw consent at any time, where processing is based on consent
Automated decisionsNot be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect you, with some exceptions
Data portabilityReceive your data in a commonly used format and move it to another provider

The right concerning automated decisions is directly relevant to AI: it means that significant decisions about people should not be left entirely to algorithms.

Breaches and accountability

A personal data breach occurs when personal data is lost, stolen, accessed without authorisation or disclosed wrongly. Under the Act, a controller must notify the NDPC of a breach likely to risk people’s rights and freedoms within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, and must inform affected individuals promptly, in plain language, where the risk is high. Serious violations can attract significant fines, calculated as a fixed sum or a percentage of annual gross revenue, whichever is greater. Individuals who believe their data rights have been violated can complain to the NDPC.
12.3:
What happens to what you type

When you type into an AI tool or upload a file, your input is sent to the provider’s servers. Depending on the tool and your settings, it may be stored in your conversation history, used to train future models, and in some cases reviewed by people working for the provider to improve safety and quality. Free consumer versions generally offer fewer protections than institutional or business versions. The provider’s privacy policy and settings explain what happens.

What not to share

A simple rule: do not enter anything into a public AI tool that you would not be comfortable seeing outside your control.

Generally safeThink firstDo not share
General questions; public information; your own notes and drafts without personal detailsYour own personal information; unpublished work; institutional documents not marked confidentialOther people’s personal data; learners’ names, results or records; passwords and PINs; BVN, NIN and account numbers; confidential or examination materials

If you need AI help with material containing personal data, anonymise it first: remove names and replace them with labels such as “Student A”, and remove other identifying details such as matriculation numbers, locations and unusual characteristics.

Privacy settings and data controls

Most AI tools let you view and delete your conversation history, and many let you opt out of having your conversations used for training. Some offer temporary or incognito chats that are not saved. Check the settings of the tools you use, and review them occasionally, because options change.

Handling learners’ data as a future teacher

As a teacher, you will be entrusted with personal data about learners, most of them children: names, ages, results, attendance, family circumstances and sometimes health or special needs information, which is sensitive data. Using AI to help analyse results or write reports may be tempting. Do it only with anonymised data and within your school’s policies, never paste identifiable learner information into a public AI tool, and never let AI make judgements about individual learners without your review.
12.4:
Digital footprint and reputation

Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online: posts, photos, comments, likes, and the data collected by apps and websites. Much of it is permanent; deleted posts may already have been copied or screenshotted. Employers, scholarship panels and school administrators increasingly look at candidates’ online presence. Before posting, ask whether you would be comfortable if a future employer, a learner or a learner’s parent saw it.

Online safety

Students are frequent targets of online fraud. Phishing messages pretend to come from banks, universities, scholarship schemes or employers and try to make you click a link or reveal passwords, PINs or one-time codes. Common warning signs include urgency (“your account will be blocked today”), offers that are too good to be true, unfamiliar links and requests for codes. Protect your accounts with these habits:

Account security essentials

  • Use a strong, different password for each important account; a long passphrase of several random words is strong and memorable.
  • Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking and social media.
  • Never share one-time codes, PINs or passwords, with anyone, for any reason.
  • Check links and sender addresses before clicking; go to official websites directly instead.
  • Keep your phone’s software updated and install apps only from official stores.

Respectful online conduct

Digital citizenship includes treating others with respect. Cyberbullying, meaning repeated harassment, humiliation or threats online, causes real harm, and group chats and social media can make it spread quickly. Hate speech targeting people for their ethnicity, religion or other characteristics harms individuals and communities. AI tools add new risks, such as creating fake images of real people to embarrass or harass them. Do not create, share or forward such content, and report it where you see it.

Legal context

Several online behaviours are criminal offences in Nigeria. The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015, amended in 2024, covers offences such as unauthorised access to computer systems, identity theft and impersonation, online fraud, and cyberstalking. The NDPA protects personal data, and the Copyright Act 2022 covers online infringement.
12.5:
Critical consumption

Responsible digital citizens think before they share. Before forwarding a message, especially one that is shocking, urgent or claims to be “breaking news”, apply the verification habits from 10.3: check the source, look for confirmation from reliable outlets, and search images. When unsure, do not forward.

Digital wellbeing

Many apps are designed to capture as much attention as possible, through endless feeds, notifications and recommendations driven by AI. Practical habits help: turn off non-essential notifications, keep the phone away during study sessions and at night, and notice how particular apps make you feel.

Helping others

Digital skills bring a responsibility to share them. Showing a family member how to recognise a phishing message, turn on two-factor authentication or check a suspicious story is a practical contribution. As a teacher, you will be in a position to build these habits in a whole generation of learners.

Key idea

Share the minimum, protect what you hold, and think before you post, paste or forward.
13.1:
Tasks versus jobs

Headlines often ask which jobs AI will “take”. A more useful way to think is in terms of tasks. Every job is a bundle of tasks, and AI affects tasks in three different ways:

Text version of Figure 13.1

More AI ← → More human

AutomateAugmentHuman-led
Transcribing a recordingDrafting lesson notesComforting a distressed learner
Formatting a reference listDifferentiating a worksheetManaging a classroom
Marking multiple-choice testsAnalysing class resultsMeeting a worried parent
  • Automation: AI performs the task with little human involvement, such as transcribing a recording or sorting routine enquiries.
  • Augmentation: AI helps a person do the task faster or better, while the person directs and checks it, such as drafting a report or analysing survey results.
  • Human-led: the task depends on human presence, judgement, relationships or physical skill, such as comforting a distressed learner or negotiating with a community.

Most jobs contain tasks of all three kinds. When some tasks are automated, the job usually changes rather than disappears, and time shifts towards the tasks that remain. Jobs made up mostly of automatable tasks face the greatest disruption. At the same time, AI creates new tasks: checking AI output, designing AI-supported processes and explaining AI to others.

Sectors most affected

Unlike earlier waves of automation, which mainly affected manual and routine work, generative AI particularly affects knowledge work: writing, analysis, administration and communication. Sectors where significant change is expected include administration and clerical work, customer service, marketing and content creation, translation, software development, finance, and education. Forecasts of how many jobs will be affected, and how quickly, vary widely between studies. The honest position is that the direction of change is clear but its size and speed are uncertain.

New roles

AI is also creating roles: specialists who train and evaluate AI systems; people who design prompts and AI workflows for organisations; AI ethics and governance officers who assess risks and ensure compliance with laws such as the NDPA; data analysts and data engineers; and trainers who help others adopt AI. Many more existing roles now include AI-related responsibilities, such as a teacher who coordinates AI use across a school.
13.2:
The AI-augmented teacher

AI can support many of a teacher’s tasks. It can help plan lessons and schemes of work, create materials, examples and practice questions, differentiate materials for learners at different levels and with different language needs, draft feedback on learners’ work, and reduce administrative burden such as drafting letters and reports. Teachers who use AI well can spend less time on routine preparation and more on teaching itself. Teachers who use it badly risk inaccurate materials, generic lessons and misjudged feedback. The skills taught in this course are what make the difference.

What remains human

The central work of teaching is relational. Learners learn best from teachers who know them, believe in them, notice when something is wrong, and adapt in the moment. AI cannot build a trusting relationship with a class, exercise moral judgement about a particular child’s situation, manage a classroom, mentor a struggling learner, or model the character and values that learners take from the adults around them. These human elements become more important, not less, as AI takes on routine tasks.

Key idea

AI will change what teachers do. It will not replace what makes good teachers matter.

Edtech and education entrepreneurship

Education graduates are well placed for work in educational technology (edtech): designing learning content, testing products with learners, training teachers, and advising companies on curriculum and pedagogy. Combined with the entrepreneurial skills of Modules 8 and 9, subject and teaching expertise can also be the basis of independent ventures: tutoring services, learning materials, teacher training and educational content.
13.3:
AI literacy and tool fluency

AI literacy, meaning understanding what AI can and cannot do, is the foundation. Tool fluency, the practical ability to use AI tools effectively in your field, builds on it. Specific tools will change; the underlying skills of clear prompting, critical evaluation and responsible use carry over from one tool to the next.

Human skills

As AI takes on more routine cognitive work, the skills it does least well become relatively more valuable:

SkillWhy it matters more with AI
Critical thinkingSomeone must judge whether AI output is accurate, relevant and sensible
CommunicationExplaining, persuading, listening and adapting to people remain human work
CreativityFraming new problems and combining ideas in original ways
CollaborationMost valuable work is done in teams, with people from different backgrounds
Ethical judgementDeciding what should be done, not only what can be done

Digital skills

Beyond AI, broader digital skills are expected in most professional roles: working with data in spreadsheets, creating digital content such as documents, presentations, graphics and short videos, and collaborating online through shared documents, video meetings and project tools.

Lifelong learning

Because tools and jobs will keep changing, the ability to keep learning is itself a key skill. Many free and low-cost options exist: short online courses from universities and technology companies, professional certifications, webinars, and communities of practice. Self-directed learning, which means setting your own learning goals, finding resources and practising, is made easier by AI tutors, but still requires discipline.
13.4:
Remote and freelance work

The internet allows people to work for clients and employers anywhere. Freelance platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr connect workers with clients for tasks such as writing, editing, design, tutoring, data work and virtual assistance. Success depends on building a reputation through ratings and reviews, which takes time; competition is global and intense; and receiving international payments in Nigeria can involve fees, exchange-rate issues and platform restrictions. Be alert to scams, such as “jobs” that require you to pay a fee first or ask for your bank details.

The creator economy

The creator economy refers to people earning income from content they create and share online: educational videos, podcasts, blogs, online courses and paid communities. Education is one of the most popular content areas. AI helps creators produce scripts, graphics and edits more quickly, but audiences value authenticity, expertise and consistency, which AI cannot supply. Most creators earn little at first; income usually comes after a long period of regular, useful content.

Nigerian and global opportunities

Nigeria has one of Africa’s largest technology ecosystems, with a young, digitally active population and growing demand for skills in technology, data, digital marketing and online education. Government and private initiatives offer digital-skills training, often free. Globally, organisations seek people who combine digital and AI skills with subject expertise and good communication. Opportunities are real, but they reward skill, reliability and patience, not shortcuts.
13.5:
Personal skills audit

Planning starts with an honest picture of where you are. A skills audit lists the skills your intended career needs, rates your current level, and identifies a next step for each:

SkillCurrent level (1–4)EvidenceNext step
Prompting and evaluating AI output2Prompt log from this courseBuild a prompt library for lesson planning
Spreadsheets1None yetComplete a free spreadsheet basics course; build a class record sheet
Presenting3Class presentationsVolunteer to present at a departmental seminar
Content creation2Social media postsCreate three short educational videos in my subject

Building a learning plan

Choose two or three priority skills from your audit, set a specific goal for each with a realistic timeframe, identify the resources you will use, and decide how you will show the result, ideally as a portfolio item (Module 14). Review the plan each semester. Small, steady progress is more sustainable than an ambitious plan abandoned after a few weeks.

Using AI for career development

AI can help you prepare for opportunities, as long as the final content is accurate and genuinely yours:

Example prompt

Here is my CV and the advertisement for a graduate assistant teacher position. Suggest how to make my CV more relevant to this role. Do not invent any experience or qualifications; only reorganise and reword what is there, and tell me which requirements I have not yet shown evidence of. [paste CV and advertisement]

Example prompt

Act as an interviewer for a secondary school teaching position. Ask me one question at a time, including at least two about classroom management and one about using technology. After each answer, give brief feedback and a suggestion for improvement.

Never include false claims in a CV or application, whether written by you or by AI. Employers verify qualifications, and dishonesty discovered later can end a career.

Key idea

Think in tasks, not jobs. Build the human skills AI lacks, keep learning, and show what you can do.
14.1:
Purpose

A portfolio is a selected collection of your work, with explanation and reflection, that provides evidence of your skills and learning. A transcript says you passed a course; a portfolio shows what you can actually do. For AI-related skills in particular, a portfolio is more convincing than a certificate, because it shows how you used AI, how you checked it and what you produced.

Types of portfolio

TypePurposeAudience
Learning portfolioDocuments your development over a course, including drafts and reflectionsLecturers; yourself
Professional portfolioPresents your best work to show your capabilitiesEmployers; scholarship panels; clients
Project showcasePresents one project in depth, from problem to resultClients; collaborators; judges

The portfolio for this course is primarily a learning portfolio, but many of its items can later be moved into a professional portfolio for teaching practice and job applications.

Platforms

A portfolio can be as simple as a well-organised folder or as polished as a personal website. Common free options include Google Sites (simple websites linked to Google Drive), Canva (visual portfolios and presentations), Notion (organised pages and databases), LinkedIn (professional profile with featured work), GitHub (for code and technical projects) and Behance (for design work). Choose a platform you can access and update easily, including from your phone, and that your intended audience can open without difficulty. Keep a backup copy of everything.
14.2:
Selecting artefacts

An artefact is a single piece of work in your portfolio. Choose artefacts that together show the range of skills in this course, for example:

ArtefactSkills it showsRelated module
A prompt library with before-and-after examplesPrompting and iteration5
A document, presentation or spreadsheet made with AI supportProductivity with AI; verification6
A study guide or research summary with verified sourcesStudy and research with AI7

A reflection on an ethical, integrity or data-protection issueResponsible use10–12
A skills audit and learning planCareer planning13

Quality matters more than quantity. Five well-documented artefacts are more convincing than twenty unexplained files.

Documenting process

For AI-assisted work, the process is as important as the product, because anyone can generate a polished product with AI. What distinguishes your work is how you directed, checked and improved it. Each entry should therefore show:

Portfolio entry: Revision spreadsheet for a JSS 2 class

ArtefactA spreadsheet that calculates totals, grades and class averages for 40 learners, with a chart of grade distribution.
PurposeTo reduce the time needed to compile continuous assessment records during teaching practice.
ProcessDesigned the columns myself; used AI to write the grading formula; built the chart; tested with sample data.
AI useAsked ChatGPT for a nested IF formula and an explanation of it (prompts in appendix).
VerificationThe first formula gave a B for a score of exactly 70. I found the error by testing edge cases and changed > to >=.
ReflectionSee the reflection below.

Showing responsible use

Your portfolio should demonstrate the habits of Module 10: disclosure of AI use in each entry, verification of facts and outputs, and protection of personal data. Do not include other people’s personal information, real learners’ names or results, or confidential documents. Use anonymised or invented sample data instead. Credit sources and any images you did not create.
14.3:
Reflection structure

A reflection explains what you learned from a piece of work, not just what you did. A simple and widely used structure has three questions:

QuestionWhat to write
What?Briefly describe what you did and what happened
So what?Explain what it means: what you learned, what surprised you, what worked or did not and why
Now what?State what you will do differently or next as a result

Showing growth

Good reflections show change. Compare your first attempt with your final version, or your understanding at the start of the course with your understanding now. Specific evidence, such as a weak early prompt set beside an improved one, shows growth far more convincingly than a general statement that you “learned a lot”.

Honest evaluation of AI’s contribution

Be honest about what AI did and what you did, including where AI helped a great deal and where it failed. A reflection that says AI produced everything perfectly suggests either that you did not check or that you did not learn much. A reflection that identifies AI’s errors and explains how you caught them shows exactly the judgement this course aims to build.

Sample reflection

What? I built a spreadsheet to calculate grades, using AI to write the grading formula. So what? The formula looked correct and worked for most scores, but gave the wrong grade at exactly 70. I would not have noticed if I had not tested boundary scores. I learned that a formula that runs is not necessarily correct, and that the edge cases are where errors hide. Now what? I now test every AI-written formula with boundary values before using it, and I have added a test section to my template.
14.4:
Planning a demonstration

A demonstration shows an audience what you made and how. Plan three things: its purpose (what the audience should understand or be convinced of), its audience (their background and interests) and its time (demonstrations usually overrun; plan for less than the time allowed). Choose one or two artefacts to show in depth rather than rushing through everything.

Presenting clearly

A simple structure works well: the problem you addressed, what you made, how you made it (including AI use and verification), what you learned, and what you would do next. Show the work itself rather than describing it. If you demonstrate live, prepare for failure: poor connectivity, a dead battery or an AI tool giving an unexpected answer. Keep screenshots or a short recording as a backup, and practise at least once with the device you will use.

Answering questions confidently

Questions are an opportunity to show understanding. Listen to the whole question, pause before answering, and answer directly. If you do not know, say so and explain how you would find out; this is more credible than guessing. Expect questions about your AI use: which parts you did yourself, how you checked the output, and what you would do without AI. Being able to answer these clearly is strong evidence that the work is genuinely yours.
14.5:
Review criteria

Portfolios are commonly reviewed against criteria such as the following:

CriterionWhat reviewers look for
QualityAccurate, well-made artefacts that meet their stated purpose
VarietyEvidence across the range of skills in the course
ReflectionSpecific, honest reflections that show learning and growth
IntegrityClear disclosure of AI use; verified content; credited sources; no personal data
PresentationClear organisation, easy navigation, readable and professional appearance

Peer feedback

Reviewing a classmate’s portfolio improves your own, because you see alternative approaches and apply the criteria critically. Useful feedback is specific (points to a particular item), criterion-based (linked to the review criteria) and actionable (suggests what to change). A helpful pattern is: one strength, one question, one suggestion. When receiving feedback, listen without defending, ask for clarification if needed, and decide afterwards which suggestions to act on.

Improving and maintaining your portfolio

A portfolio is never finished. After the course, keep adding your best work from other courses, teaching practice and personal projects; replace weaker items with stronger ones; update reflections as your understanding grows; and remove anything outdated. A portfolio maintained throughout your degree becomes a powerful resource when you apply for teaching positions, further study or other opportunities.

Key idea

Show the product, the process and the judgement. Anyone can generate output; your portfolio shows what you did with it.
15.1:
Part A · Understanding AI · Modules 1–5

  • AI is the ability of computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence; machine learning, deep learning and generative AI are nested subsets of it.
  • Common myths: AI understands, is always right, will replace all jobs, is neutral, is only for experts.
  • AI developed in cycles of optimism and “winters”; it matured now because of data, computing power, algorithms, investment and accessibility together.
  • All current AI is narrow AI. Machine learning learns patterns from data: supervised (labels), unsupervised (clusters), reinforcement (rewards). Overfitting means memorising rather than generalising.
  • LLMs predict the next token; this makes them fluent but prone to hallucination, bias, outdated knowledge and inconsistency.
  • Effective prompts combine role, task, context, format and constraints; output improves through iteration.

Part B · AI for Productivity and Learning · Modules 6–7

  • AI can draft, edit and structure documents, plan and draft presentations, and write and explain spreadsheet formulas. Use AI as an editor, not an author, and test formulas with edge cases.
  • Retrieval practice and spacing are among the most effective study methods; AI makes quizzes, flashcards and timetables easy to create.
  • AI can fabricate references. Use academic search tools, open every source, and evaluate sources for authority, currency and relevance.
  • AI should support your thinking, not replace it. Follow course rules and keep a prompt log.

Part C · Entrepreneurship and Opportunity · Modules 8–9

  • Entrepreneurship is identifying opportunities and taking initiative to create value; types include business, social, intrapreneurship and edupreneurship.
  • The entrepreneurial mindset includes initiative, resilience, creativity, calculated risk-taking and a growth mindset.
  • Opportunities come from problems, changes, gaps and new technology. Screen ideas for need, market, feasibility and resources.
  • Start from problems, not solutions. Use observation, open interviews, surveys and secondary research. Design thinking: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test.
  • Validate assumptions cheaply with prototypes before building.

Part D · Responsible and Lawful Use · Modules 10–12

  • Core AI ethics principles: fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, human oversight.
  • Bias enters through data, design and deployment; removing sensitive features does not remove it because of proxies.
  • Verify before sharing; deepfakes and AI misinformation are best countered by checking sources.
  • Copyright protects expression and arises automatically; in Nigeria it is governed by the Copyright Act 2022 and administered by the NCC. Presenting AI output as your own work is misconduct; disclose and cite AI use.
  • The NDPA 2023, enforced by the NDPC, sets principles, lawful bases and data subject rights. Never enter others’ personal data into public AI tools.

Part E · Future, Practice and Assessment · Modules 13–14

  • AI affects tasks: some are automated, some augmented, some remain human-led. Jobs change more often than they disappear.
  • Teaching remains relational; AI can support planning, materials, differentiation and feedback.
  • Valuable skills: AI literacy, critical thinking, communication, creativity, collaboration, ethical judgement, lifelong learning.
  • A portfolio shows product, process and judgement; reflections follow what, so what, now what.

Section B: Short answer

Define hallucination in generative AI and give one example.

Model answer

A hallucination is output that is fluent and confident but false or fabricated. Example: an AI assistant lists a journal article, with authors, title, journal and page numbers, that does not exist. Marking points: definition (fluent/confident and false); a valid example.

State three factors that explain why AI has advanced rapidly since the 2010s.

Model answer

Any three of: large amounts of data from the internet and smartphones; greater computing power from GPUs and cloud computing; better algorithms such as deep learning and transformers; heavy investment and open research; accessible interfaces such as chat apps. One mark per factor, with brief explanation.

Distinguish between overfitting and underfitting.

Model answer

Overfitting occurs when a model memorises its training data, including random quirks, and so performs well on training data but poorly on new data. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the real patterns and performs poorly on both. Marking points: each correctly defined; contrast drawn.

Write a problem statement using the user–need–insight formula for a problem of your choice.

Model answer

“Commuting students at our university need a way to study productively during long bus journeys, because they spend up to three hours a day travelling but their notes are in bulky handouts that are hard to use on a bus.” Marking points: specific user; need stated without naming a solution; insight that explains why.

List four principles of data processing under the NDPA 2023.

Model answer

Any four of: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; storage limitation; accuracy; integrity, confidentiality and security. One mark each.

Give two reasons why an AI-detection score alone should not be treated as proof of academic misconduct.

Model answer

AI detectors produce false positives, flagging genuine human writing, and have been found to flag second-language writers more often; they can also be evaded, so their scores are unreliable in both directions. Two valid reasons.

Section C: Essay and scenario

“AI will replace teachers.” Discuss this statement.

Marking points

  • Introduction that frames the question in terms of tasks rather than whole jobs.
  • Tasks AI can automate or augment: planning, materials, differentiation, feedback drafts, administration, with examples.
  • What remains human: relationships, judgement about individual learners, classroom management, mentoring, modelling values.
  • Risks of poor AI use: inaccurate materials, over-reliance, data protection.
  • Reasoned conclusion, for example that teaching will change and AI-literate teachers will be advantaged, but teachers will not be replaced.

A secondary school teacher pastes her class’s names and examination scores into a free AI chat assistant and asks it to write a comment on each learner’s report card. Identify the issues this raises and advise her on a better approach.

Marking points

  • Data protection: learners’ names and results are personal data of children; entering them into a public tool may breach the NDPA principles and school policy; the data may be stored, used for training or reviewed.
  • Quality and fairness: AI comments may be generic, inaccurate or biased, and do not reflect her knowledge of each learner.
  • Accountability: the teacher remains responsible for every comment.
  • Better approach: anonymise data (Learner A, B), or use AI only to draft general comment templates; personalise and review every comment herself; follow school policy on AI tools.

Using the stages of design thinking, explain how a group of students could develop a solution to a problem faced by first-year students on campus.

Marking points

  • Empathise: observation and open interviews with first-year students; example findings.
  • Define: a clear problem statement using user, need and insight.
  • Ideate: generating several possible solutions before choosing; AI may support brainstorming.
  • Prototype: a quick, cheap version such as a paper mock-up or a manual trial.
  • Test: trying the prototype with real users; iterating based on feedback; the loop may return to earlier stages.

  • Structure longer answers: jot a brief plan, use paragraphs with one main point each, support points with examples, and end with a conclusion that directly answers the question.
  • Use course terms precisely: examiners reward accurate use of terms such as “hallucination”, “data minimisation” or “augmentation”.
  • Do not leave blanks: attempt every required question; partial answers earn partial marks.

Integrity in examinations

The principles of Module 11 apply fully in examinations. Unauthorised materials, communication with others, and the use of phones, smart devices or AI tools during an examination are serious misconduct, with penalties that can include cancellation of results. The purpose of the examination is to show what you have learned, and the best preparation is the steady, active study this course has described.

Key idea

Revise by recalling, not re-reading. In the examination, answer the question asked, using the language of the course.
